e.meaning: from the Austrian capital, a name probably of Celtic origin
e.etymology: From the capital of Austria. Vienna is the Italian and Latin form of German Wien, a name probably of Celtic origin, perhaps from a word for wood.

assoc.t: capital of Austria
Vienna sausages, small canned sausages
Vienna, Billy Joel's 1977 song

e.etymology: From Latin Rosalia, the Roman festival of roses, from rosa, rose. Saint Rosalia is the 12th-century patron saint of Palermo, Sicily.

assoc.t: Rosalia, Grammy-winning Spanish pop star

e.etymology: From Hawaiian ke, the, and anu, coolness. Actor Keanu Reeves has explained his name as cool breeze over the mountains.
namesakes: Keanu Reeves (actor, The Matrix and John Wick)

assoc.t: actor Keanu Reeves

e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who worked with clay or lived on clay soil, from Old English claeg. It is also a short form of Clayton.

assoc.t: clay, the earth used for pottery and bricks

e.etymology: A spelling of Muhammad, the passive participle of Arabic hammada, to praise. This form is common in Iran, the Levant and South Asia. It is the name of the prophet of Islam.

assoc.t: the prophet of Islam, usually spelled Muhammad

e.etymology: From the Scottish surname McKinley, Gaelic Mac Fhionnlaoich, son of Fionnlaoch, fair warrior. It was briefly popular for boys when William McKinley was president and returned in the 2000s as a girls' name.

assoc.t: William McKinley, 25th US president
Mount McKinley (Denali), North America's highest peak

e.etymology: From Hebrew chayah, living, the feminine counterpart of Chaim. It is a traditional name in Orthodox Jewish families. An unrelated Indian name, Chhaya, is Sanskrit for shadow.
e.note: The Hebrew ch is a throaty kh sound; English speakers often say it with the ch of chair.

e.etymology: The Basque spelling of Amaya, the heroine of an 1879 historical novel by Francisco Navarro Villoslada, usually linked to Basque amai, end. Amaya is also the name of a mountain and village in northern Spain.
From Old Norse Gunnarr, built from gunnr, battle, and a word for army or warrior. Gunnar is a hero of the Volsunga saga; Gunther is the German cognate.
e.note: In American English it is pronounced like the word gunner.

e.etymology: From an English surname, possibly a variant of Hadley. It fits the sound of Hadley, Ashley and Addie, which helped it catch on for girls.

assoc.t: A for Adley, popular kids' YouTube channel

e.etymology: A phonetic English spelling of Sean, the Irish form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
namesakes: Shawn Michaels (WWE Hall of Fame wrestler)

e.etymology: An Irish saint's name, possibly from ceallach, strife, or from ceall, church. Saint Kilian was a 7th-century Irish missionary to Germany.
e.note: The Irish C is hard, as in Killian; Americans often misread it as SIL-ee-un.

assoc.t: Cillian Murphy, star of Oppenheimer and Peaky Blinders

e.etymology: From a Scottish surname taken from Leslie in Aberdeenshire, a place name traced to Gaelic lios cuileann, garden of hollies. Once mostly a boys' name, it is now given mainly to girls in the US.
namesakes: Leslie Knope (Amy Poehler's character in Parks and Recreation)
Leslie Nielsen (actor, Airplane! and The Naked Gun)

e.etymology: Coined by the English poet Fulke Greville around 1600 for the woman addressed in his love poems, possibly as an anagram of Mary or from Latin myrrha, myrrh.
From the Spanish and Latin word sol, sun; today it is given mostly to girls in Spanish-speaking families. In early 1900s America it was mainly a short form of Solomon.

assoc.t: sol, Spanish for sun and the Latin name of the Sun
sol, the fifth note of the do-re-mi scale
sol, a Martian day in NASA mission timekeeping
Sol, Mexican beer brand

e.etymology: The Scottish form of Old Norse Rognvaldr, built from regin, counsel, and valdr, ruler. Reginald and Reynold are its cousins.

assoc.t: Ronald McDonald, the McDonald's clown mascot
Ronald Reagan, fortieth US president

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Kennedy, from the Irish surname O Cinneide, descendant of Cinneidigh, a byname read as helmeted head or misshapen head.

assoc.t: President John F. Kennedy and the Kennedy family

e.etymology: The Japanese word kaizen, written with the characters for change and good, known in English as the business practice of continuous improvement. Its use as a given name is recent and American.

assoc.t: kaizen, the business method of continuous improvement

e.note: In Japan kaizen is an everyday word and a workplace term, not a traditional given name.

e.etymology: A short form of Jason, the Greek hero's name, traditionally tied to the Greek verb for to heal. Its American peak in 2013 coincided with Jase Robertson's fame on the TV show Duck Dynasty.
From Arabic Layla, from the word for night. Leyla is the Turkish and Azerbaijani spelling; the name is famous from the old love story of Layla and Majnun.

assoc.t: Layla, the 1970 Eric Clapton rock song (same sound)

e.meaning: Spanish form of Julius; traditionally read as youthful
e.etymology: The Spanish form of Julius, the Roman family name of Julius Caesar. Its root is uncertain; it has long been explained as youthful or downy-bearded.

assoc.t: julio is the Spanish word for July
Don Julio tequila

e.etymology: A medieval diminutive of Leon or of the nickname Lion, from Latin leo, lion. Sir Lionel is a knight of the Round Table in Arthurian legend.

assoc.t: Lionel model trains
soccer star Lionel Messi and singer Lionel Richie

e.etymology: The Turkish form of Arabic amir, a title for a prince or commander, from a root meaning to command. It is common in Turkey and among Bosniaks.

assoc.t: emir, the title of a ruler in some Muslim countries

e.etymology: The double-l spelling of Philip, from Greek Philippos: philos, loving, and hippos, horse. It was borne by kings of Macedon and by one of the twelve apostles.
namesakes: Phillip Phillips (American Idol winner and singer)
Dr. Phil McGraw (TV host, born Phillip)

e.etymology: A pet form of Daniel, Hebrew for God is my judge, and now and then of Danielle. It has long been given as a name in its own right.

assoc.t: Danny Boy, the Irish ballad

e.etymology: The Italian form of Helios, the Greek word for the sun and the name of the sun god.

assoc.t: Elio, the boy hero of Pixar's 2025 film Elio
Elio in the film Call Me by Your Name

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that joins Jay- to the -lani ending of Hawaiian names such as Leilani and Kailani.
A modern name with no single source. It is used as a spelling of Eliana, Hebrew for my God has answered, and as a longer form of Alina.
A short form of Cleopatra, glory of the father, or a spelling of Clio, the Greek muse of history. Both come from Greek kleos, glory or fame.

assoc.t: Miss Cleo, 1990s TV psychic hotline pitchwoman
Cleo the goldfish in Disney's Pinocchio

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Charlie, the pet form of Charles and Charlotte, using the fashionable -leigh ending. Charles comes from a Germanic word for a free man.

e.meaning: French form of Mary; meaning debated: beloved, bitter or wished-for child
e.etymology: The French form of Maria, from Hebrew Miryam, the name of the mother of Jesus. English borrowed it from French, and it became one of the most common American middle names.
namesakes: Marie Curie (physicist and chemist, two Nobel Prizes)

e.etymology: An English occupational surname for a maker of arrows, from Old French fleche, arrow.
namesakes: Fletcher Christian (leader of the mutiny on the Bounty)

assoc.t: FLETCHER, the pop singer
